questions.stem: Read: „Liebe Oma, wir sind gestern in Wien angekommen. Das Wetter ist herrlich und das Hotel liegt direkt am Prater. Bis bald, deine Mia“ What type of text is this?
options: An advertisement for a hotel
A formal letter of complaint
A diary entry for herself
A postcard to a relative
questions.explanation: The informal greeting „Liebe Oma“, the holiday news and the signature „deine Mia“ mark a postcard. A diary is not addressed to anyone and is not signed off.

questions.stem: Read: „Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, am 3. März habe ich bei Ihnen eine Jacke bestellt. Leider ist sie bis heute nicht angekommen. Ich bitte Sie, mir den Betrag zurückzuerstatten.“ What does the writer want?
options: Her money back
A different jacket
A faster delivery
A discount on her next order
questions.explanation: „Den Betrag zurückerstatten“ is to refund the amount. She is not asking for the jacket to be sent faster; she wants to cancel and be repaid.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of a German diary entry, „ein Tagebucheintrag“?
options: Numbered steps and instructions in the imperative
The first person, a date, and the writer's feelings
A formal greeting to the reader and a signature at the end
A headline, a by-line and quotes from experts
questions.explanation: A diary entry is dated, written as „ich“ and personal. Headlines and quotations belong to a newspaper article, and numbered imperatives to instructions.

questions.stem: Which sentence suits a factual report, „ein Bericht“, rather than a personal blog?
options: Am Samstag nahmen rund 200 Schüler an dem Lauf teil.
Ich war sooo müde, aber es hat echt Spaß gemacht!
Mir hat der Lauf ehrlich gesagt total gut gefallen.
Ehrlich, ich hatte am Anfang null Lust auf den Lauf.
questions.explanation: A report gives facts in the third person, usually in the imperfect: who, what, when. The others use „ich“, feelings and casual words such as „sooo“ and „null Lust“.

questions.stem: Why does a written German story usually say „er ging“ and „sie sah“ rather than „er ist gegangen“ and „sie hat gesehen“?
options: The imperfect is used only for events that happened long ago
The perfect is used only with the verbs haben and sein
The imperfect is the normal past tense for written narrative
The perfect is incorrect for any events in the past
questions.explanation: Speech mostly uses the perfect, but written narratives and reports use the imperfect. The perfect is not wrong; it simply belongs to conversation, emails and letters.

questions.stem: Why do German recipes often give instructions as infinitives, as in „Die Butter schmelzen“?
options: It is a polite form used to address older readers
It shows that the steps can be done in any order
It shows that the recipe has been copied from an older cookbook
It is the impersonal convention for written instructions
questions.explanation: Recipes, manuals and signs („Bitte nicht rauchen“) use the infinitive as an impersonal instruction, addressing no one in particular. The order of the steps still matters.

questions.stem: In a letter of application, which sentence is out of place?
options: Na, alles klar bei euch?
Anbei finden Sie meinen Lebenslauf.
Hiermit bewerbe ich mich um die Stelle.
Über eine Einladung würde ich mich freuen.
questions.explanation: „Na, alles klar bei euch?“ is casual, uses „euch“ and belongs in a message to friends. The other three are standard formal phrases in a „Bewerbung“.

questions.stem: In a text message, „Treffen uns um 8 vorm Kino, ok?“, what does „vorm“ stand for?
options: für den
vor dem
vor den
von dem
questions.explanation: Informal writing contracts „vor dem“ to „vorm“, as standard German does with „im“ and „zum“. „Von dem“ contracts to „vom“, and the plural „den“ never contracts.

questions.stem: A school newsletter article begins „Endlich Sommerferien!“ What does the exclamation do?
options: It asks the reader a question
It apologises to the reader
It grabs the reader's attention with enthusiasm
It tells the reader the exact dates of the summer holidays
questions.explanation: An exclamation as a heading engages the audience, one of the stylistic features the study design names. „Endlich“, 'at last', adds relief and excitement.

questions.stem: An advertisement says „Hol dir jetzt die App!“ What does the „du“ form tell you?
options: It is aimed at business customers
It is a translation from English
It is meant for older readers who expect a formal tone
It is aimed at young people in a casual tone
questions.explanation: „Hol dir“ is the du-imperative, which advertisers use to sound friendly to a young audience. A formal ad would say „Holen Sie sich …“.

questions.stem: Read the blog: „Mein Tag ohne Handy: Am Anfang war ich total nervös und habe ständig in meine Tasche gegriffen. Am Abend habe ich aber gemerkt, dass ich viel mehr mit meiner Familie geredet habe.“ How did the writer's day go?
options: Nervous at first, then she noticed a benefit
Relaxed at first, then more and more nervous
Nervous all day, so she gave up by evening
Happy all day because she had lost her phone
questions.explanation: „Am Anfang“ sets up the nervous start, and „am Abend … aber“ turns to what she gained: more talk with her family. Reaching into her bag was habit, not a lost phone.

questions.stem: Read the review: „Der neue Film von Lena Hoff ist optisch beeindruckend, doch die Handlung zieht sich. Nach neunzig Minuten wartet man immer noch darauf, dass etwas passiert.“ What is the reviewer's view?
options: It is impressive in every single way
It looks impressive, but the story drags
The story is gripping, but it looks dull
It is far too short to tell its story
questions.explanation: „Optisch beeindruckend“ praises the look, and „doch die Handlung zieht sich“ criticises the plot as slow. Ninety minutes with nothing happening makes the point.

questions.stem: Read: „Könnten Sie mir bitte mitteilen, ob es noch freie Plätze gibt und wie viel der Kurs kostet?“ What does the writer want to know?
options: When the course starts and where it is held
Whether the course is free and who teaches it
How many people have enrolled and the price
Whether places remain and what the course costs
questions.explanation: Two indirect questions follow „mitteilen“: „ob es noch freie Plätze gibt“, whether places are still available, and „wie viel der Kurs kostet“. „Freie Plätze“ are free places, not a free course.

questions.stem: In an article: „Wer möchte schon in einer Stadt leben, in der man nicht mehr atmen kann?“ What is the purpose of this question?
options: To ask readers to send in their opinions
To find out which city readers would most like to live in
To introduce an interview with a resident
To persuade, since it implies that nobody would
questions.explanation: It is a rhetorical question: no answer is expected, and „schon“ signals that the answer is obviously 'nobody'. It pushes readers to agree with the writer.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an indirect question?
options: Der Kurs beginnt, wenn alle da sind.
Wer hat am Sonntag schon Lust auf einen Kurs?
Sie wollte wissen, wann der Kurs beginnt.
Wann beginnt der Kurs am Montag?
questions.explanation: An indirect question is reported inside another sentence, with its verb at the end: „…, wann der Kurs beginnt“. „Wenn“ in the third sentence introduces a condition, not a question.

questions.stem: Tim asks „Kommst du am Samstag mit?“ How do you report his question?
options: Er fragt, ob ich am Samstag mitkomme.
Er fragt, wenn ich am Samstag mitkomme.
Er fragt, ob komme ich am Samstag mit.
Er fragt, dass ich am Samstag mitkomme.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question becomes indirect with „ob“, 'whether', and the verb goes to the end, so the prefix rejoins it: „mitkomme“. The person also shifts from „du“ to „ich“.

questions.stem: Read: „Immer mehr junge Menschen verzichten auf ein eigenes Auto. Gründe sind die hohen Kosten, aber auch das wachsende Umweltbewusstsein.“ What is the main idea?
options: Young people are buying more electric cars
More young people are choosing not to own a car
Young people cannot afford to buy petrol
Cars are becoming much better for the environment
questions.explanation: „Verzichten auf“ is to do without, so the general meaning is going without a car. Cost and environmental awareness are the specific reasons, not the main point.

questions.stem: Read: „Die Ausstellung ist dienstags bis sonntags von 10 bis 18 Uhr geöffnet. Montags bleibt das Museum geschlossen, außer an Feiertagen.“ Which visit is possible?
options: A Monday public holiday at 11 am
An ordinary Monday morning at 11 am
A Tuesday at 7 pm
A Sunday at 9 am
questions.explanation: „Außer an Feiertagen“ means the museum opens on Mondays that are public holidays. Tuesday at 7 pm is after 18 Uhr, and Sunday at 9 am is before opening.

questions.stem: Read: „Obwohl Paul seit Monaten für die Prüfung gelernt hatte, war er am Morgen so nervös, dass er nichts essen konnte.“ What can we tell about Paul?
options: He was well prepared but very nervous
He had not studied and was nervous
He was calm because he had studied
He was ill and could not eat for months
questions.explanation: „Obwohl … gelernt hatte“ concedes that he had studied for months, and „so nervös, dass …“ gives the result. The months refer to studying, not to being unable to eat.

questions.stem: Read: „Wir laden alle Eltern herzlich zum Sommerfest am 20. Juni ein. Für Kuchen ist gesorgt; Getränke bitte selbst mitbringen.“ What should parents bring?
options: A cake and some drinks
Plates and cutlery
Their own drinks
A cake to share
questions.explanation: „Für Kuchen ist gesorgt“ means cake has been taken care of. „Getränke bitte selbst mitbringen“ asks parents to bring their own drinks.

questions.stem: Read the recipe: „Die Butter schmelzen, dann Zucker und Eier unterrühren. Den Teig 30 Minuten ruhen lassen, bevor er in den Ofen kommt.“ What happens just before baking?
options: The dough rests for 30 minutes
The butter is melted for 30 minutes
The eggs are beaten for 30 minutes
The oven heats for 30 minutes
questions.explanation: „Ruhen lassen“ is to let rest, and „bevor er in den Ofen kommt“ places it right before baking. Melting the butter is the first step, not the last.

questions.stem: Read: „Hallo Herr Wagner, leider kann ich am Montag nicht zur Probe kommen, da ich einen Arzttermin habe. Viele Grüße, Lea“ Why will Lea miss the rehearsal?
options: She is going on holiday
She has to work on Monday
She has a doctor's appointment
She has an important exam on Monday
questions.explanation: „Da“ here means 'because', and „einen Arzttermin“ is a doctor's appointment. „Die Probe“ is a rehearsal, not a test.

questions.stem: Read: „Clara Schumann (1819–1896) war eine der bekanntesten Pianistinnen ihrer Zeit. Sie komponierte auch selbst und war mit dem Komponisten Robert Schumann verheiratet.“ Which statement is true?
options: She was Robert Schumann's daughter
She was a composer but did not perform
She was born in the twentieth century
She was a pianist who also composed
questions.explanation: „Pianistinnen“ makes her a pianist, „komponierte auch selbst“ a composer too, and „verheiratet“ means she was married to Robert, not his daughter. The dates place her life in the nineteenth century.

questions.stem: Text A: „Das Jugendzentrum bietet ab Mai kostenlose Gitarrenkurse an.“ Text B: „Ich will unbedingt Gitarre lernen, aber Unterricht ist mir zu teuer. – Jonas“ Why would Text A interest Jonas?
options: The courses start in May
The centre lends out guitars
The courses are for beginners
The courses cost nothing
questions.explanation: Jonas's problem is cost, „zu teuer“, and „kostenlos“ means free of charge. The May start is true but does not answer his problem, and neither text mentions loans or levels.

questions.stem: Text A: „Ferienjob im Café am See: Juli und August, nur am Wochenende.“ Text B: „Ich suche einen Job für die Sommerferien, kann aber nur unter der Woche arbeiten. – Sara“ Does the job suit Sara?
options: Yes, it is during the holidays
No, it is only in July
Yes, it is close to where she lives
No, it is only at weekends
questions.explanation: „Unter der Woche“ is on weekdays, and the job is „nur am Wochenende“. The holiday timing fits, but the days do not, so the general match hides a specific mismatch.

questions.stem: Text A: „Konzert im Stadtpark, Samstag 19 Uhr, Eintritt frei.“ Text B: „Am Samstag muss ich bis 18:30 Uhr arbeiten, und ich habe kaum noch Geld. – Ben“ Could Ben go?
options: Yes, it starts after work and is free
No, it clashes with his work
No, he cannot afford the tickets
Yes, but only if he leaves work early
questions.explanation: He finishes at 18:30 and the concert starts at 19 Uhr, and „Eintritt frei“ means no ticket to pay for. Both of his problems are answered by details in Text A.

questions.stem: Read: „Im Winter lieben wir die Gemütlichkeit: Kerzen, Tee und ein gutes Buch.“ What does „Gemütlichkeit“ convey?
options: A strict daily routine
A sense of loneliness
A busy social life
A warm, cosy, relaxed feeling
questions.explanation: „Gemütlichkeit“ is comfort, warmth and ease together, which no single English word covers. The candles, tea and book in the text give the picture.

questions.stem: Read: „Nach Feierabend trifft sich mein Vater gern mit Kollegen.“ What is „der Feierabend“?
options: The evening before a holiday
A celebration at work
The end of the working day
A party on the weekend
questions.explanation: „Feierabend“ is the time after work finishes for the day; „Feierabend machen“ is to knock off. Despite „feiern“, to celebrate, it need not involve a party.

questions.stem: Read: „Du hast die Prüfung nicht bestanden! – Na und? Ich mache sie im Herbst noch einmal.“ What attitude does the second speaker show?
options: Unconcerned: 'So what?'
Angry with the first speaker
Surprised by the result
Ashamed of the result
questions.explanation: „Na und?“ is 'so what?', shrugging off the news, and the plan to resit in autumn confirms it. Nothing shows anger or surprise.

questions.stem: Read: „Hast du keinen Hunger? – Doch!“ What does the reply mean?
options: I've already eaten
Yes, I am hungry
No, I'm not hungry
I don't know yet
questions.explanation: „Doch“ contradicts a negative question or statement: 'yes, I am'. „Nein“ would agree with the negative and mean 'no, I'm not'; English has no single word for this.

questions.stem: Read: „Toll, schon wieder Regen. Genau das, was ich für mein Picknick brauche.“ What is the writer's tone?
options: Grateful
Indifferent
Sarcastic
Delighted
questions.explanation: „Toll“ and „genau das, was ich brauche“ say the opposite of what is meant, since rain ruins a picnic. Read literally, the text sounds delighted, which is the trap.

questions.stem: Read the headline: „Schule ohne Noten – Chance oder Risiko?“ What will the article most likely do?
options: Weigh up arguments for and against
Report one school's exam results
Give instructions to teachers
Advertise a private school
questions.explanation: „Chance oder Risiko?“ sets up two sides, which signals a discussion. „Noten“ here are marks, so a school without them is the topic, not exam results.

questions.stem: Read: „Der Autor bezweifelt, dass das neue Gesetz etwas ändern wird.“ What does the author think?
options: The new law will change everything
The new law should be changed by parliament soon
The new law is too complicated
The new law probably won't change anything
questions.explanation: „Bezweifeln“ is to doubt, from „der Zweifel“. Mistaking it for „befürworten“, to support, reverses the author's view.

questions.stem: Read: „Das Hotel war zwar teuer, aber das Frühstück war hervorragend.“ What is the writer saying?
options: The hotel was cheap, and the breakfast was excellent
The hotel was expensive because the breakfast was so good
The hotel was expensive, and the breakfast was poor
The hotel was expensive, but the breakfast was excellent
questions.explanation: „Zwar … aber“ concedes one point and then sets another against it: 'admittedly expensive, but'. „Hervorragend“ means outstanding.

questions.stem: In a survey report, what does „knapp die Hälfte der Befragten“ mean?
options: Almost all of those asked
Just under half of those asked
Just over half of those asked
Exactly half of those asked
questions.explanation: „Knapp“ before a quantity means just under, and „gut die Hälfte“ would be a good half, just over. „Die Befragten“ are the people surveyed.

questions.stem: In an article, what does „fast jeder Dritte“ mean?
options: Nearly three in four
Nearly one in three
Nearly a third of the time
Almost every third day
questions.explanation: „Jeder Dritte“ is one person in three, and „fast“ makes it 'nearly'. Three in four would be „drei von vier“.

questions.stem: Read: „In der Stadt werden jedes Jahr Tausende Bäume gepflanzt.“ What does this mean?
options: Thousands of trees will be planted in the city next year
Thousands of trees were cut down in the city last year
The city wants to plant thousands of trees one day
Thousands of trees are planted in the city every year
questions.explanation: „Werden … gepflanzt“ is the present passive, here for something that happens every year. It does not name who plants them, which is what the passive is for.

questions.stem: Read: „An deiner Stelle würde ich früher losfahren.“ What is the writer doing?
options: Making a complaint
Apologising
Describing a past trip
Giving advice
questions.explanation: „An deiner Stelle“ is 'in your place', and with „würde“ it means 'if I were you, I would'. It is a polite way of giving advice.

questions.stem: Read: „A: Wollen wir heute Abend ins Kino? B: Ach, ich weiß nicht. Ich bin ziemlich kaputt. A: Schade. Dann vielleicht morgen?“ What happens?
options: B is too tired, so they might go tomorrow
B's television is broken, so they stay in
A is too tired, so B goes alone
They agree to go to the cinema tonight
questions.explanation: „Kaputt“ said of a person means exhausted, not broken. „Schade“ accepts the refusal, and „vielleicht morgen“ suggests another day.

questions.stem: Read: „Da es seit Tagen regnete, wurde das Fußballturnier verschoben.“ What happened?
options: It rained there for days after the tournament
The tournament was moved to another town by the rain
The tournament was postponed because of days of rain
The tournament went ahead although it had rained
questions.explanation: „Da“ at the start of a clause means 'since' or 'because', and „verschieben“ is to postpone. Reading „da“ as 'there' loses the cause.

questions.stem: Read: „Viele finden, Jugendliche sollten weniger Zeit am Handy verbringen. Ich sehe das anders: Gerade dort lernen wir, uns zu organisieren.“ What is the writer's position?
options: She has decided to spend less time on her phone
She disagrees with the common view and sees a benefit
She agrees that young people should use their phones less
She thinks phones are useful only for adults
questions.explanation: „Ich sehe das anders“ is 'I see it differently', rejecting the view of „viele“. „Gerade dort“, 'precisely there', points to the benefit she claims.
